speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some questions to direct to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs who, even if the roster applied, would be expected to be here on Thursday, but in his absence I must direct the questions to the Prime Minister. speechtext:
that Bill C-231, to provide for the resumption and continuation of longshoring and grain handling operations and operations related to longshoring or grain handling at ports on the west coast of Canada be read the second time and referred to the Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, no one will regret more than I the necessity of introducing this legislation to the House. The bill that we have under consideration today provides for the resumption and continuation of longshoring operations and, if necessary, grain handling operations at ports on the west coast.
This government, and indeed predecessor governments, does not wish to deprive trade unions, employers and employees of the full rights of collective bargaining. But there are occasions when Parliament must deal with situations, when the full resort to economic warfare by strike or lockout so impairs the ability of others to carry on their activities that it can be said to be against the national interest for the work stoppage to continue. Parliament in this case was recalled as a last resort when it was evident that the ports on the west coast would not resume operations for some weeks if normal collective bargaining procedures were allowed to take their course.

August 31, 1972
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
I do not think any honourable member will deny that a critical and urgent situation exists in western Canada as a direct result of the cessation of the longshoring operations of the ports on the coast of British Columbia. Already damage to the economy of Canada is evident and will mount at an increasing rate the longer the ports are closed. By far and away the hardest hit at this time is the grain economy on its external markets. This important sector of the economy is presently in the greatest jeopardy should the ports remain closed. British Columbia, too, has an export-oriented economy, and it is of the utmost importance that there be no prolonged closure of its ports. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said when he announced the recall of Parliament,
This government does not intend to permit the benefit gained by all Canadians from its international efforts to be dissipated by a prolonged closing of the ports.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF LONGSHORING, GRAIN HANDLING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT WEST COAST PORTS
speechtext: When did he arrive at that view?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF LONGSHORING, GRAIN HANDLING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT WEST COAST PORTS
speechtext:
The Canadian Wheat Board has undertaken very large sales commitments to Russia and China, in addition to its regular sales to Japan and other nations. Indeed, our capacity for moving grain has been overstrained to meet these commitments. This export movement of grain has been concentrated through the port of Vancouver which has now been closed for 25 days.
The Asian market has been of growing importance for Canadian grain sales and has greatly enhanced the significance of shipments through the west coast ports, principally Vancouver. But one very important element in grain marketing, as it is in other businesses, is the ability of the seller to deliver on schedule. If our customers cannot depend on our shipments they will look to competitors, which can result in the permanent loss of markets. It is estimated that Canada's shipments have fallen behind by 30 million bushels and it will take a great deal of effort and additional cost to catch up. Any further delay in the resumption of operations will make it virtually impossible to do so. Not only have shipments fallen behind, but our grain transportation facilities are seriously dislocated and it is anticipated that it will take up to one month to get grain moving normally again. Future sales may well be precluded or lost by the inability of the system to deliver at a time when delivery capacities are already over-taxed by high sales volumes and catch-up efforts.
Mr. Speaker, it is perhaps desirable at this point for me to give hon. members the background of the dispute affecting the longshoring operations. I am going to say something further in a few moments about another dispute, the second dispute which complicates the first and that is the dispute with respect to grain handling operations as opposed to longshoring operations. In the case of the longshoring dispute, the previous collective agreement expired on July 31, 1972, between the British Columbia Maritime Employers' Association, which represents some 61 member companies in collective bargaining, and the International Longshoremen's and Warehousemen's Union, which through various locals, represents some 3,300 longshoremen employed by these companies, at the ports of Vancouver, New Westminster, Chemainus, Port Alberni, Victoria and Prince Rupert.

Direct negotiations between the parties took place on five occasions during May and June. No agreement was reached. On June 7, the union requested the appointment of a conciliation officer. Two west coast officials of my department were appointed, but they were unsuccessful in bringing the parties to an agreement. The conciliation officers recommended the appointment of a conciliation board which I did appoint on July 24 with Dr. Noel Hall of Vancouver as chairman. The board met with the parties on July 26, 27 and 28 and reported to me on July 31.
The report, which was unanimous, indicated that the board felt it could serve no useful purpose at this stage because one party to the dispute took the position that meaningful progress toward resolving the dispute could only be made through direct talks between the parties.
Despite the fact that the board was unable to make recommendations on the substance of the matters in dispute, the chairman held himself available to assist the parties in any way possible and obtained an agreement from the parties that they would seek the assistance of the board before there was any breakdown in direct negotiations. The report was released to the parties on August 1, 1972 and, pursuant to the Labour Code, the parties were in a position to strike or lock-out on Monday, August 7 at midnight.
On August 6, complications arose affecting the port of Vancouver only, when longshoremen on regular work assignments resigned and reported for work on the daily despatch that applied to all other longshoremen at Vancouver. The dispute involving the despatch of the men has not been resolved and the port of Vancouver has remained closed since that date.
Various efforts to halt this work stoppage were made by the parties themselves and by my officers, but these met no success. Efforts were also made during this time to work out arrangements with the unions, as was done in 1969, to load grain on a voluntary and temporary basis through the National Harbours Board. The union, however, desired a permanent collective agreement arrangement with the board or another governmental agency to replace the agreement covering this work with the British Columbia and Maritime Employers' Association. The union's proposal had far-reaching implications which would require an extensive study which could not be commenced, let alone completed in the time available. Accordingly, the government felt that it could not accept the union's proposal.
Dr. Hall made further efforts to seek a solution to the dispute, but he was unable to do so. On August 10 and 11 the union took a strike vote of its membership employed at all west coast ports which authorized the union executive to take strike action. The remaining five ports were struck on August 23.
Well before that date, on August 14, I sent Mr. W. P. Kelly, Assistant Deputy Minister of Labour, to Vancouver to assist Dr. Hall and to discuss other avenues to settlement. Again, no progress was made in the resolution of the dispute concerning despatching.
The day following the general shut-down of the west coast ports, I travelled to Vancouver and met with the representatives of the employers and the union. The first
August 31, 1972

meeting took place jointly. Subsequently meetings took place separately.
At the time of my arrival on the west coast, there were no negotiations in progress. Both parties agreed to meet and did so the following and subsequent days. Both parties desired some days of direct discussions because the complex issues involved in the dispute had not previously been explored. Neither party wished to have the assistance of my officials, but they agreed to meet daily and to make progress reports to me daily. While the atmosphere of the meetings appeared to be good, the parties could not assure me that an agreement would soon be forthcoming. Therefore, it became the government's view that the emergency which already existed could only deepen while collective bargaining proceeded over a period of several weeks.
The bill before the House provides for the resumption of longshore and related operations on the west coast while the parties continue to bargain for a settlement of their dispute. It provides for the extension of the collective agreement to December 1972, or until the parties make a new agreement, whichever is earlier. It also provides for further mediation. Strikes or lockouts during the extended term of the agreement are prohibited by the legislation.
Hon. members will observe, Mr. Speaker, that there are two main parts to the bill. Part I deals with the longshore dispute. Let me now deal with Part II of the bill which parallels in most respects Part I. There are separate and distinct operations from longshoring involving grain movement which are carried on in Vancouver by five elevator companies. Some 500 employees of these companies are represented by the International Union of Brewery, Flour, Cereal, Soft Drink and Distillery Workers of America. Part II of the bill before us applies to these operations in contrast to Part I which applies to the longshore operations which do indeed involve grain as well as other commodities moving to the ports.
At the outset, I wish to point out particularly that this part comes into effect only on proclamation, and I hope that no proclamation will be necessary. The present situation in this dispute is that the collective agreement between the elevator companies and the union expired on November 30, 1971. Since that time extensive negotiations have been conducted and the conciliation officer and conciliation board procedures have been complied with and followed. The conciliation board reported to me on August 16, 1972 and the report was released to the parties and made public on the same day. Thus a strike or lockout could legally have commenced at midnight on August 23, about a week ago. The companies have rejected the recommendations of the majority of the board. The union accepted the recommendations, but desired some clarification from the chairman of the board. The chairman of the conciliation board has very recently supplied the information requested and it was remitted to the companies and the union yesterday.
I do expect that the parties to the second dispute, this elevator and grain handling dispute, will reach an early settlement. Regretfully, though, it will not be in time to
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
relieve the government of the obligation to deal with this situation in the bill now before the House. It is, therefore, essential that when port operations do resume as a consequence of part one of this bill the movement of grain should not be disrupted again by failure to reach agreement on the second dispute. If there should be a settlement of the second dispute, I repeat, there will be no proclamation with respect to part two of the bill. Because an early settlement of the longshore dispute is not apparent-indeed, it does not seem apparent in the next several weeks-and because of the critical situation in western Canada and in British Columbia in particular arising from the halting of shipments of grain, potash and other commodities from the prairie provinces, and of lumber, mineral and other products from British Columbia, it has been necessary to introduce this bill. I should add that in British Columbia the stoppage of loading operations has paralysed coastal shipping carrying supplies to remote ports and islands.
The basic purpose of the bill before us is simple. It is to bring about a resumption of port operations while negotiations continue toward a settlement. It is to interfere as little as possible with the collective bargaining process. It is to leave the parties, as they wish to be left, to negotiate directly, and, with the assistance of mediators, to arrive at an agreement which they can live with and want to live with during the next period. I sincerely regret that for the reasons outlined to the House there is no practical alternative to the adoption of the bill before us. Mr. Speaker, I now move its second reading.

government has spent much of its time emasculating Parliament, when we consider that the denigration of Parliament was, for a while at least, the favourite indoor sport of this government, I suppose that what is happening here today must be regarded as a victory of sorts. But now the government is forced to call Parliament back if it wants to settle anything in connection with this matter. Unfortunately, however, there is a darker side to this picture because this government's decision to recall Parliament, after it has failed to take any action itself over a period spanning several years and when it saw its last few western seats slipping from its grasp, has to be qualified as a sordid piece of cynicism.
I hope that no one is under any illusion that the bill which has been presented today really offers any solutions to these deep-seated labour problems. Certainly, it offers no solutions to the problem of the disputes in the public service or in essential services in general. It is no secret that we are in danger of witnessing yet another postal strike in the next few months. I am not predicting that this will happen, but we are all aware that this may very well happen. The only comment I would care to make at this time on this subject is that if this strike should materialize during the long-promised election campaign that we are expecting, that is if there should be a stoppage of certain postal services during that campaign, then this Parliament has already given to the government the means with which to delay a general walkout until a new government can take over after the election and work out a satisfactory solution to these difficulties. If I understood the minister today, they are not likely to be proclaimed for some time because of the dithering around by the minister. I do not know what his real reasons are for not wishing to proclaim the provisions of the Labour Code after they were passed at the last session. However, I want to make it very clear to everybody concerned that Parliament at that time did give the government the authority to deal, during the period of dissolution with stoppages of the sort, by order in council where it was deemed in the national interest. We would be interested to know whether, in fact, the government does proceed to proclaim this legislation.
I recognize that there is no simple solution to the problems of labour relations. It is a complex field, often filled with tension, and certainly the issues frequently are not easily resolved. To name but one, there is the whole matter of the response of labour and management alike to technological change. This is a factor in both the British Columbia strike and the current postal negotiations. It is one element, and there are others, which demonstrates that labour disputes will become even more complex, and perhaps even more difficult of solution, in the future than they have been in the past. That is why we must all be constantly on the lookout for new ideas and new approaches.
There are many who strongly urge a resort to compulsory arbitration in the realm of essential industries and services, whether they be in the public or the private sector. Something like this may have to come with regard to essential services. I say this very reluctantly, not only because this would be a further limitation on freedom but

That is why I believe we should certainly try other methods, and that is why any government that I would lead would take urgent steps to set up a public interest disputes commission to deal with the problem of essential services. I do not say that this is a magic wand, but I can see that in this situation, for example, such a commission could have played an active and constructive role in anticipating these difficulties and in trying to resolve them long before the contracts were to expire, and long before the difficulties which resulted in a work stoppage came to a head. Such a public interest disputes commission, consisting of men and women with wide experience in the field who know the problems and who are independent in their thinking, could, even without compulsion, play an active role. The recommendations of such a body would have a degree of moral force that would make anybody, employer, union or government, think twice before ignoring them.
I believe that such a public interest disputes commission could play an active part in reducing substantially the kind of tie-ups and stoppages that have been occurring in essential services, both public and private. I believe that is the kind of policy that the government should have been working out and long since should have had in operation. That is the kind of activity that would have earned the gratitude of Canadians and even the respect of the opposition, at least the respect of the members of my party. That, I believe, is the direction in which the government should have been going. This would not be a cure-all but an active measure that does not restrict freedom but one that would lead to the reduction of tensions and the resolution of disputes in advance of actual breakdown.
The government did not take that course. That is one reason we are back here today, faced again with this kind of difficulty as a result of this government's incompetence. Whatever may be the reasons, we are faced with a measure on which we must take some decisions. I am certain the voters of Canada will recognize that the timing of this particular piece of legislation was entirely political, and has much more to do with the possibility of the coming federal election than with the welfare of Canada and the welfare of Canadians. I am confident that the voters will not be fooled by what the government has done. I want to spend my time, which I hope will not be too long, in dealing with, (a) the general subject with which the bill is concerned, and (b) the bill itself.
The questions which I asked earlier during the question period with regard to whether or not the parties were informed of the government's intention, and whether the government knew that a new proposal was going to be made, were simply directed to the point that a government which does not have the foresight and the courage to draw to the attention of parties in a serious dispute that it considers the dispute serious and will act if it is not settled, is escaping its obvious duty.
I am certain that if the parties to this dispute had been informed by the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell), or by his officers in British Columbia, that the government considered that the dispute had to be settled, and that if it were not settled by the parties then Parliament had no alternative but to act, there was a strong possibility that they themselves would have settled it and Parliament would not have had to act. It is this kind of failure on the part of the government that I find very condemnable indeed.
I am told by Mr. Garcia, the president of the union-I mention him so that nobody will have to guess at the source of my information-that in the presence of the Minister of Labour the two sides to the dispute agreed to meet solidly for seven consecutive days for the purpose of trying to reach a settlement. If the minister agreed to that, and if he got the parties to agree to such a procedure to
August 31, 1972

undertake seven days of negotiation, what is the labour movement to think when the government does not give it seven days to do that which the minister had asked it to do? What kind of position does the Minister of Labour hold when he gets the parties to make a serious effort at negotiating a settlement, and two days after that agreement is reached the parties, without any previous warning, are faced with Parliament being recalled and legislation being placed on the books?
I suggest that the major problem facing us in the realm of labour relations is that, even though the Department of Labour has some very competent people in it, the direction of that department is incompetent. The direction of that department is unimaginative. The direction of that department is without policy, with the result that we jump from crisis to crisis in serious labour relations matters without knowing exactly where we are going, how we are going to get there, and why we should try to get there. When the present Minister of Labour was appointed to that portfolio, even though I recognized his kindness, his decency and his sincerity, I questioned whether his particular experience had qualified him for such a sensitive job. I am afraid that what has happened since his appointment has underlined the reasons for that questioning.
This is the second time within two months that Parliament has had to act to order people back to work. I can think of nothing I dislike more, and that my colleagues dislike more, than Parliament ordering men and women to go back to work when they are not satisfied with the conditions under which they work. I find that totally repugnant to any idea of democracy and democratic behavior. For the government to put Parliament in a position where it has no alternative than to do this seems to me to be really reprehensible. I cannot guarantee that this situation would not have arisen, but I do know that the officers of the department who were in Vancouver were simply sitting and watching the parties negotiate, and that when the minister went out to Vancouver he simply watched them talk and had a little chat with them. Mr. Speaker, when you are faced with a serious labour matter, that kind of behavior is irresponsible incompetence.
When you are faced with a serious labour relations situation, one in which you eventually intend to pass a law ordering people back to work, then sitting on a chair, or whatever it was that the officers of the department sat on-some of it too indelicate to mention-and just hoping that the parties will be nice to each other, is not good enough. Effective and active intervention by the officers and effective and active intervention by the minister, banging the table, talking to the parties, pointing out the seriousness of the situation to them, warning them of action that Parliament might have to take, arguing with them about the issues that are involved, all these are the tasks of the Labour Department, and particularly of the minister, in a situation which may end in Parliament ordering people back to work. This total incapacity to understand its obligations and duty in such labour relations matters is another indication of the arrogance and the complacency with which the government regards important matters.
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
On June 30, we passed Bill C-183 dealing with the Canada Labour Code, in which we made provision to deal with some of the matters that were in dispute on the west coast, and that were in dispute at the Quebec ports in the strike which we dealt with at the beginning of July. But to date that law has not even been proclaimed, and the minister tells us that he does not intend to proclaim it in the near future or, that if he proclaims those provisions, he will change the rules in the middle of negotiations. I happen to know that one of the things that management asked for in its latest offer last Tuesday was that the employers be exempted from certain provisions of that bill which have not yet been proclaimed. That was one of the matters which the union had to face, a demand by management that its members lose the safeguards and seniority that are presently in the collective agreement with respect to job security for members of the work force on the west coast.
We would be in a different situation if that bill had been proclaimed. I want to draw to the attention of Parliament, and to the attention of everybody else interested, that the amendments to the Canada Labour Code which we passed provide that technological change is subject to negotiation even during the life of a collective agreement; that it is subject to conciliation, and that it may be an issue on which people may strike. We write that into the law. We write into the law the right to strike and we write into the amendments to the law the right to strike in the case of technological change, then, owing to the inadequacy of the actions of the Department of Labour, the moment workers exercise it we say, "You can't; get back to work." I am worried when that kind of thing happens because nothing undermines the observance of the law and respect for the law so quickly and so easily as for people to be given a right solemnly by Parliament and when they exercise that right, to be told by Parliament "You can't. Sure, we gave you the right to strike but we didn't really mean it. When your strike becomes effective we are going to pass a law and order you back to work." That is the kind of action that produces disrespect for the law and makes workers and members of unions in this country feel that the law is not really ever on their side.
Mr. Speaker, that is not good; that is destructive of the democratic process. I condemn this government for having permitted the situation to continue to the point where Parliament is forced to do just that, to tell the people who exercise a right that we gave them that they cannot exercise it any longer. And why? Because it has become effective. People suffer as a result of a strike, which in a sense is precisely what a strike is for, and since the strike has become effective we tell them that they cannot continue it any longer, that they have to get back to work. This is what we must avoid, and in order to avoid it, I repeat what I have said many times in this House. The federal Department of Labour must become much more streamlined, must stop watching these crises develop hoping that everything will come out all right and then when it does not, bringing a bill into this House. The minister, and the very able officers of his department, have to stop this game of passivity and become active participants in the settlement of serious disputes so that

August 31, 1972
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
we will not again have to go through this exercise twice in two months.
The issues on the west coast are basically the same as the issues in Quebec or the issues in Britain and the rest of the world, as they relate to longshoremen. I am told money is not involved, that there could easily have been a settlement on any increase in wages. The real problem is the introduction of automation, computerization and assignment of work, the introduction of technological changes which are perhaps necessary for society as a whole but which threaten the security of the jobs of the people involved. As a Parliament, we cannot say to workers in a particular industry that they have to carry the full load of technological progress from which society as a whole will benefit and from which employers will benefit by added productivity, as well as perhaps added profitability, that the workers are to take it on the chin, losing the security of their jobs and becoming the victims of automation and technological change. That is the situation now, and we as Members of Parliament and the people of Canada must realize that even though the strike of the workers on the west coast has to be ended because it has reached the point where it is harmful to many other Canadians in this country, I want to say on behalf of my colleagues and myself that I hope the people of Canada will recognize that the longshoremen have a right to be concerned about the effects of technological change on their situation and their job security, and that they have a right to fight for security in their jobs-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF LONGSHORING, GRAIN HANDLING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT WEST COAST PORTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF LONGSHORING, GRAIN HANDLING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT WEST COAST PORTS
speechtext:
-and to expect from their employers in the first place, and from the Parliament of Canada in the second place, some kind of protection of their life work and the welfare and future of their families.
This is the issue that this Parliament will have to face sooner or later. If, from time to time, we are going to take away the right to strike, it is not enough merely to have a provision in the Labour Code that technological change should be a matter of negotiation and in the end people can strike, because that right is worthless if the right to exercise it is taken away. I suggest, therefore, that Parliament will have to deal with the question of the effect of technological change and the need to protect the working people of this country who would be the victims of such change.
Mr. Speaker, I think that in this bill the mediator ought to have been given, by law, instructions to deal with the effects of technological change in a way which would protect the security of the jobs of the longshoremen on the west coast. I intend that either one of my colleagues or myself will move an amendment to this effect in committee of the whole. I hope the minister will consider it carefully, and perhaps agree to it, so that the people involved on the west coast will feel that they have received some justice. Before I indicate exactly the point I am driving at, let me put it in a general social or philosophical context.
When there is a lawful strike, a strike in accordance with the provisions of the law, and for reasons of the welfare of all the people of Canada or some section of the people, Parliament considers it necessary to end that

strike by law and order the people back to work, I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that those people have a right to have in the law some kind of quid pro quo. They have a right to have in the law some provision that justifies ordering them back to work. Merely to make them go back to work until the end of December under the old agreement and keep on negotiating to arrive at a new agreement is not enough. It is very dangerous from one point of view as far as the working people are concerned. That point of view is the retroactivity of any settlement made in these negotiations. The last agreement terminated on July 31. If you permit negotiation to be carried on without anything in the law guaranteeing or protecting these people in their rights to retroactive application of any term as a condition of the new agreement, then you give the employer an immense weapon and the employees and union have no weapon at all. For the next few months, if the employers do not like what is going on they have the power just to sit there and say no, but the employees from whom this bill takes away the right to strike until January 1, have no power at all at the negotiating table between now and the end of the year. They just sit there and argue as best they can, but if the employer does not want to budge there is nothing they can do about it because the threat of a strike has gone until January 1, and a strike in the coming winter is a great deal more difficult than a strike in August.
I, therefore, appeal to the minister and all members of this House that if we are going to pass this bill, and it will be passed because, for the same reason as every other member in this House we are forced to support it as reluctantly I am sure as everyone else because of the west coast situation, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, we have a social obligation to put into it something that will protect the workers, that will reduce the power of the employers in the next three or four months and put a little bit of power in the hands of the negotiating committee and the working people. I believe that this bill, in the appropriate sections, ought to contain a simple provision that any agreement arrived at by the parties as a result of the negotiations that the law requires them to enter into or any terms thereof, shall, unless the parties otherwise agree be retroactive to August 1,1972.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF LONGSHORING, GRAIN HANDLING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT WEST COAST PORTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF LONGSHORING, GRAIN HANDLING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT WEST COAST PORTS
speechtext:
I know the arguments, Mr. Speaker. I have had enough experience in labour relations. I am sure some of the minister's officials know that retroactivity is a matter of negotiation. Sometimes the union sells retroactivity for some other benefit it wants to get and all the rest of it. I suggest to the minister that words can be found to enable that. That is why the amendment which we would move, and I hope the minister will move it, will say that the terms of the agreement or any of them shall be retroactive to August 1, 1972, unless the parties to the agreement agree otherwise. They can negotiate. They can agree on certain benefits, such as wages, going back to August 1 and some other benefits being retroactive to November 1 or some other time. It is up to them to decide. The grain handlers could have the benefits retroactive to
August 31, 1972

November 30 or November 1, 1971, when their agreement ended.
I appeal to the minister and all Members of Parliament. Unless this kind of protection is given to longshoremen, they have none at all. All that Parliament will have done will be to postpone the problem for four months. That is all they will have done. We will not have accomplished anything except to enable the government to enter into a federal election without the anger of people with regard to this strike on the west coast. When that anger comes back on January 1, 1973, it will be after the election has been held.
That is all this bill does. However, because it does make it possible for the grain shipments to start again, every member of this House, myself included, feels compelled to give assistance and support to this bill. I repeat, however, that we have a moral and a social obligation to make sure that it is not only one side in the dispute that will get hurt as a result of this bill.
As this bill is now worded, only the longshoremen will get hurt. The employer will not get hurt. He does not have to worry about retroactivity. As far as the employer is concerned, work will resume on the basis of the old collective agreement and the longshoremen will have exactly the same as they had before. The employer will not lose anything by the passage of this bill. The working people will lose. They will lose their power to force upon their employer the conditions of work they would like to have. In return for that loss to the longshoremen on the west coast, this Parliament has an obligation to assure in the law that the employers will not be able to play cat and mouse with the question of retroactivity.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF LONGSHORING, GRAIN HANDLING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT WEST COAST PORTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF LONGSHORING, GRAIN HANDLING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT WEST COAST PORTS
speechtext:
I raise this out of an actual experience I have had with the longshoremen on the west coast. I forget exactly when it happened. Two, three or four years ago, there was a voluntary return to work while negotiations continued. The minister nods his head indicating that he knows about it. It was three years ago. I have been informed by the union officials that the employees lost $2 million in wage increases that the employers refused to make retroactive. They lost certain provisions with regard to their pension plan, contributions to the pension plan that were going to be improved and so on.
The longshoremen on the west coast have a right to demand of Parliament that this little bit of justice be done. If they are to be forced back to work, the law should guarantee to them that the managers and employers cannot get around this. The law should guarantee the retroactivity of any benefits which are negotiated in the collective agreement.
I wish to say a few words about part of the bill that applies to grain handlers. The grain handlers have a right to feel aggrieved by the proposition of this bill because they have accepted the conciliation board report. It is the employer, including, I am sorry to say, the Saskatchewan and Alberta wheat pools that have rejected the conciliation board report. To threaten them with action in case they should strike, even before they have taken a vote, seems to be a pretty serious matter. As far as I know, they have not even taken a vote to strike. I may be wrong on
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
that. The minister has indicated that I am right. To threaten them in their situation with this kind of action if they should strike is serious.
The grain handlers' contract expired almost a year ago. It expired last November, 10 months ago. They are working without any new or revised collective agreement. They have gone through all the procedures. It took them months to do this. They have accepted a conciliation board report. This bill gives the government the power to order them back to work when the government thinks it is necessary, without any protection of their welfare. This seems to me to be an immoral act which the minister ought not make this Parliament perpetrate.
In the case of the grain handlers, we should have the same amendment requiring that the provisions of any new agreement, unless otherwise agreed to by the parties, become retroactive to either November 1 or November 30. I cannot remember whether it is the beginning or the end of November. The parties can agree to change that with regard to any provision they have to make.
I did not take any longer than I needed to make the thoughts of my colleagues and myself as clear as I have been able to make them. There is no reason why we should be in this kind of crisis every two months. There is no reason at all. We are in this kind of crisis because of a totally wrong approach to labour relations by this government. I have made that statement many times in the past number of years. This attitude that not only is justice blind, but the labourers in the ports must be blind and have blinkers over their eyes until they and everybody else are kicked into seeing something that any half intelligent person, even this government, could have foreseen is just not good enough.
I believe we will not solve this problem, leaving alone the whole problem of the handling of grain, until this Parliament deals with one matter, namely automation and technological change and unless this government or whatever government follows it has the courage and the vision to make the federal labour department an active participant in important labour disputes, instead of a passive observer.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF LONGSHORING, GRAIN HANDLING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT WEST COAST PORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have carefully listened to the comments of the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) concerning new techniques or automation. He also told us that the bill does not solve per se the problem now under consideration.
Mr. Speaker, the longshoremen's strike on the west coast has been lasting for a few weeks, that is a little too long. The government dispatched the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) to British Columbia and I feel that the latter, during his recent visit in Vancouver, has particularly contributed to the campaign for the election of a New Democratic government.
Mr. Speaker, in fact he went over there and came back to tell the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) this: It

August 31, 1972
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
is impossible to solve the problem; they do not want to make sense. And so, we were ordered back to Ottawa on the double to study and pass legislation ordering the longshoremen of the west coast back to work.
Mr. Speaker, to my mind, the government was a little late in acting to settle the dispute, it knew full well that the negotiations were leading nowhere. The minister or ministers should have been sent to help solve the conflict between stevedores and employers. Today, we face an alarming situation. Hundreds of ships stand at anchor in the port of Vancouver; they can neither be loaded nor unloaded. The western farmers are waiting to ship their wheat; all is at a standstill; no solution has been found.
Mr. Speaker, the government is now introducing a bill to compel the longshoremen to resume work without making any suggestion so that bargaining may lead to agreement between both parties. The government does not give any advice. It merely says: Go back to work! Mr. Speaker, this is putting an artificial leg in a cast. Just telling workers to get back to work not later than December 31 means that we may still face the same situation on January 1.
We have had the same thing in Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec City, not so long ago. We called for government intervention. But they said: We must not interfere, even if the strike must last for weeks and months. Longshoremen in Montreal, Quebec City and Trois-Rivieres, as well as their families, have suffered all this time, but the minister kept answering every day: I do not want to interfere. And yet, at that time, there was an emergency in those ports.
Today, they tell us: They could have used the ports of Sorel, etc. What a farce! Everybody knows that longshoremen in Montreal, Quebec City, Trois-Rivieres belong to the same unions as those in Sorel. They would not have tolerated that situation. They would not have agreed to get back to work. The minister was well aware of that. However, it took weeks and months before some action was taken. Now, in this case, there is immediate intervention to settle the dispute.
Hence, people are wondering whether the government has two sets of attitudes and policies, one for the people of western Canada and another for the people of eastern Canada, especially in Quebec. That is what we are objecting to. We want the same policy implemented in the province of Quebec, the Maritimes, etc. We want the same policy of justice for the workers to be applied all across Canada whether in Vancouver, Halifax, Montreal, Trois-Rivieres or Toronto.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-231 is not the solution to the problem. We know we will have to begin all over again, for the same causes generally produce the same results. He who sows carrots cannot expect to reap potatoes. He who sows cauliflowers reaps just that, not bananas. Most of the time, the same causes produce the same effects.
These conflicts, whether in Vancouver, Toronto, the province of Quebec or Manitoba or elsewhere, all stem directly from an economic system which does not take reality into account and which we try to adapt to the requirements of a small number of financiers who control the flow of the economic blood of the Canadian people

and create chaos in various areas of the country. Instead of improving the system or establishing a better one, you punish the workers, the managers, in short, everybody.
Mr. Speaker, as long as we do not adopt a system whereby individual security would be closely dependent upon the production of our nation, we shall run around in circles as we are doing now. The end of a strike will see the beginning of a new one and there will be no end of it. We are acting just like a dog chasing its tail and running around in circles: we will never find a solution.
I heard the leader of the New Democratic Party say that we must ensure job security for the longshoremen and grain handlers in Vancouver, even if new techniques, computers, etc. are used.
Mr. Speaker, it is intended to add job security to the purchase of new machinery. Then let's talk about price and salary controls and see whether that will give prosperity to Canada, whether the Canadian people will be able to benefit from their production!
In fact, we have got new machines, we have got computers. We are using new machinery. But as intelligent Canadians-and not as people lost in confusion-we must ask ourselves: Will their use penalize man or serve him?
If all that has been devised to punish mankind, let us keep up our present system since everything is well and fine. Conflicts regarding grain, dissatisfaction, upheavals, attacks here and there, interunion struggles, union members fighting other unions, lay-offs and unemployment are instances of the uneasiness resulting from this system.
Mr. Speaker, if inventions, technology, computers and new machines have been devised to punish mankind, let us keep to our present course, since we are doing very well. If, on the other hand, these new inventions, techniques, computers and machines are to serve man and not subdue him, there is but one solution which is, not to provide job security, but income security which is the only means of facing up to the situation.
The following conclusion could thus be drawn, Mr. Speaker: if new technology, inventions, machines and computers are called upon to perform workers' jobs- which is actually the case against which both workers and unions are rebelling-briefly, if all these things are to serve mankind, there is only one way to proceed. To the extent that these innovations are put into operation, let us give everyone an income based on the productivity in Canada of these new machines and new technology, an income which would be synonymous with economic and social security, or a national dividend, whatever the name, provided a balance can be struck between the purchasing power and the country's productivity.
It is then, Mr. Speaker, that we would have a balanced economy rather than witnessing such situations as are now occurring not only in Vancouver, but also in many other places. There are lay-offs taking place, for instance, near Contrecoeur, at General Motors, Northern Electric, among longshoremen of national harbours and postal workers.
Dissatisfaction is rampant everywhere. Why? Because people want security and rightly so. The only way to do it
August 31, 1972

is not by collaring and forcing them to occupy a position which is redundant, but to give them the necessary purchasing power to buy whatever products machines are going to produce for them. Then only, would we show respect for man who was certainly not created and born only to be put to work for the sake of working-at cutting branches along highways, for instance, or doing winter works or local initiatives or Opportunities for Youth projects in which hardly anything is ever built and which have no purpose other than keeping those people working and earning a living.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the biggest mistake I ever saw, for you cannot help people in this way as you could logically do by making available to them the means to go and seek the existing production in Canada.
In order to solve those problems, Mr. Speaker, the money issue is not the only thing to be taken into account; there is also the matter of how to come to terms in the field of labour-management relations. I do not intend to go into this in detail, as my colleague from Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne), who was a union president for years, will deal in depth with the matter of labour-management relations.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that a Canadian labour court be created as soon as possible in order to prevent disputes and to maintain the best possible relations between labour and management. This, of course, will require the co-operation of union leaders if unions are to be conciliators, not distributors of boxing gloves.
Managers, who are human beings the same as workers, do not want to be molested or lose their freedom any more than workers do. In order to satisfy both, we would therefore need a Canadian labour court made up of representatives of unions, management and government-in short, unbiased people who really seek solutions to labour problems.
Mr. Speaker, this is the proposition we are making; my colleague from Kamouraska and other colleagues will give more details. However, I would like to say there is only one way to a valuable solution, that is to take into account new techniques, as the member for York South was saying, but not by submitting human beings or workers to a technology that will increase the cost of production without liberating man. Such is real democracy. We are here to govern on behalf of the human being; let us do so. Let us liberate man by the use of machines, science and progress.
Mr. Speaker, lastly I would like to say that it has been reported for some weeks that I was dying in Montreal. Others said that I was dying in Rouyn. Well, I am in parliament today and my health is probably better than that of many people who wanted me out of the way. So, I think that we will be able to go on fighting, not for our personal objectives but for the instauration of a new system in Canada. Let us change what we have so that Canadians can be assured of security and personal liberty.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is in the nature of every strike that it causes harm to persons not directly involved. We have been very conscious of the
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
fact that, in the case of the particular strike at west coast ports, there have been significant amounts of interference, harm and inconvenience caused to a large number of people. We think readily of the situation concerning grain but, of course, there are many other people involved in perhaps smaller ways individually but ways still as serious to them. Even in the Prairie region I think, for instance, of the alfalfa pelleting plants and the difficulties which surround their attempt to move small amounts of products relative to grain through the ports, but who are seriously affected by delays.
The list of those affected on the Prairies and in the west is very long, indeed, and that is the reason everyone must have serious concern about the existence of almost any strike and the inconvenience and difficulties caused to persons not directly involved. In the case of grain, a great deal has been said because of the largeness of its role in the handling of products through the west coast and also because, in the initial closing of the Port of Vancouver it was the product affected much more seriously and for a much longer period of time since a very large proportion of grain moved through the west coast does in fact move through the Port of Vancouver.
In the case of grain, part of our difficulty and problem was due to the fact that we have a program and volume of shipment out of all ports at very high levels, indeed. We completed last year a total export which is roughly estimated at about 815 million bushels of grain and the current program is even heavier than last year's. This meant that in many cases we were going to test the facilities for handling and shipping grain out of the country to the fullest at different points in time. This is particularly true in the case of the west coast.
I have made it clear before that we believe some additional facilities, storage and the like, are needed there to cope with ever larger amounts of grain moving out from the west coast to our new and old customers, large customers such as China and Japan, and customers who have been at smaller levels but extremely important such as Peru, the Phillipines and others. In the last crop year we moved approximately 308 million bushels of grain out of Vancouver, an all time high and far above previous levels. As I have said, in this particular year we have programs to attain levels even higher than that. We were in a position, therefore of needing to strain to the full to accomplish our deliveries, and an interference or delay of nearly a month can have a very serious effect in that context. In the course of that month about 30 million bushels of grain might have moved out of the west coast ports, which therefore we must attempt to move in addition to our regular programs. We will try to do so. It is important, of course, that we get the ports back into operation, and the full co-operation of the whole industry is needed, but every effort will be made to catch up in any way this can be accomplished. That is why the passage of this bill is so important in beginning the operation of catching up on our sales. Our delivery commitments may indeed be caught up if we can start the operation right away. Any longer delay and the matter would become very serious indeed.
3912

August 31, 1972
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
We will be making every effort to catch up. Prince Rupert, which has been operating at levels close to its capacity with its existing facilities, is having a second leg put into operation for the receiving of grain and will have a capacity which is perhaps double its present level. We will have to look to extra shifts and the quickest possible turnover of railway equipment if we are to catch up, and we will therefore be counting on the co-operation of everyone throughout the industry, whether they be rail-waymen, grain handling workers or elevator agents, to begin the process of moving grain to the coast. The problem of a strike is one which hurts many innocent people and it is therefore one which is open to easy criticism. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF LONGSHORING, GRAIN HANDLING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT WEST COAST PORTS
speechtext:
The problem with strikes, and the problem with doing something about them, is that since they are harmful and hurt many people they are therefore an undesirable method. Everyone agrees on the basic principle that the collective bargaining process is valuable, a process which we should try to maintain in our society. The free development by the parties themselves of their positions must be achieved. The question must be what you would put in the place of collective bargaining if you are so critical of it and want to remove it. What alternatives are there that will not interfere with the collective bargaining process itself. What alternatives are there which are sufficiently satisfactory to the men who are involved in the negotiations, alternatives which they will accept, when the strike has been so long associated by them with the need for the protection of themselves and of their rights in situations where historically they were often deprived of them.

This is the challenge, and it is not an easy one. It is easy to attempt to make political or instant capital of the desirability of settling a strike. The leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Lewis) indicated his confidence in the able officers of the Department of Labour, and I must say that with the able officers in the department and the able Minister of Labour it is a matter of their judgment as to how they can best attempt to assist the negotiations. Of course, they applied that judgment to the very best of their ability in the processes of negotiation. We are told on the one hand that we should not have waited so long, and then somehow, peculiarly, that when we make this move at this time the timing is political. It is a strange conclusion indeed and one difficult for me to understand, when presumably they mean we should have acted earlier.
The point, of course, is that we had hoped the collective bargaining process would produce a result, and we bent our efforts in that direction. The Minister of Labour has described the situation. He spoke about his officers being present at the scene. There were also descriptions of the situation when grain was one of the products not moving through the port of Vancouver, and special efforts were made to try to get it moving. When this was not possible the Minister of Labour tried to get the parties not just back to the bargaining table, in which he succeeded, but to get the product moving while they discussed the matter because the strike was bound to begin to hurt the economy, perhaps irreparably. When this was not possible, it was necessary, in the government's view, to come back to Parliament and to ask the parties to go back to work while they negotiate.
The bill is careful to preserve the basic collective bargaining principle and this is still extremely important. Anyone who could easily suggest alternatives should know what the impact of his suggestions are. There are very few countries in the world which have found successful solutions to the labour problems which can crop up. Some of the authoritarian governments have found solutions, and it is perhaps significant that they may be among the few who have, with whatever effect upon the rights and freedoms of the parties involved. In other countries a whole variety of solutions have been tried, and yet strikes go on whether legal or illegal. The collective bargaining process is important. We believe in its preservation so that the parties can discuss their problems together and can together attempt to sort out the best possible solution in the situation. It is therefore, as the Minister of Labour has said, with regret that we find it necessary at this point to interfere in the sense that we are at least indicating that the parties must go back to work while the bargaining process goes on. But the bargaining process seemed to be one which would take a significant amount of time and this would cause serious damage to many sections of the community, not only the noticeable ones but also many others which might have been noticed far less.
It is, therefore, extremely important to start the grain moving again, to solve the problems and avoid harm to many other individuals and all kinds of products, that we have the parties working while the collective bargaining goes on. Hopefully, the best kind of atmosphere and the best kind of negotiation can lead to a solution in the near future, and at that point, as the bill itself makes clear, the
August 31, 1972

operation of the bill will come to an end with the coming into place of the collective bargaining agreement. That is an end that we all desire, an end that the economic welfare of the country requires. So, we will certainly not only earnestly ask the House for support in the quick passage of this bill but also earnestly ask for the support of the parties in the discussion, negotiation and mediation process so that a successful conclusion to the work problems at the west coast may be reached. I, therefore, urge all members to support a quick passage of the bill in order that the work of the ports may begin again, and so that the harm which undoubtedly has been caused will be stopped.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR RESUMPTION AND CONTINUATION OF LONGSHORING, GRAIN HANDLING AND RELATED OPERATIONS AT WEST COAST PORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the House that I do not intend to delay passage of this important piece of legislation, but I do wish to express a few thoughts on the government's stand with respect to the present phase in the evolution of strikes and collective bargaining. The hon. member who preceded me said it is of the utmost importance that collective bargaining continue while work is being done. This piece of legislation deals in effect with two unions, the longshoremen's union and the grain handlers in Vancouver port. I point out that the grain handlers have been involved in what might be called collective bargaining since November 30 of last year. This gives some idea of how long they have continued to work without agreement on a contract.
It is interesting to reminisce on labour disputes in Canada in 1971. I do not intend to deal with the whole subject of collective bargaining, but rather with the question of government intervention to ensure that work will continue while collective bargaining takes place. According to one study something like 152,000 man days were lost through strikes and lock-outs in areas under federal jurisdiction during 1971. Those of us involved in the grain industry recently experienced a strike which lasted for about eight weeks in Quebec ports. In fact the strike at Montreal port was an illegal one, but the Department of Labour did not feel it should intervene. Now, the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) intervenes just three weeks after the start of a strike on the west coast. I can only thank democracy for the fact that we are facing an election, and elections make governments act. At election time, governments seem to realize their responsibilities more fully.
The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board mentioned alfalfa pelleting plants. There are a number of these in my constituency. Their product is in keen demand internationally. No doubt the Vancouver port tie-up is detrimental to their situation, and to farmers generally across the Prairies.
It is important that we examine the whole question of government intervention, of when government should intervene and when it should not. Earlier, in Vancouver, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) suggested that the government had given these people the right to strike, that they should be allowed to strike, and that that procedure should take its course. Now, all of a sudden, with an election coming on, he realizes he must act. I hope that the people on the Prairies and all across Canada realize he is
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
acting solely because of the election and not because of any deep-seated belief he may or may not have.
I have reached that conclusion because on July 7 Parliament passed certain amendments to the Canada Labour Code. One of those amendments gives the government the power, when a strike or lock-out is anticipated during dissolution of Parliament, to decide that a national emergency could be created, and so the government could act without recalling Parliament. That legislation has not yet been proclaimed, and this gives you some idea of the strong feelings of the Prime Minister. Here is pragmatism at work, dealing with crisis after crisis as they arise.
The Prime Minister is not concerned with the crisis on the Prairies; he is concerned with the forthcoming election. He is not concerned with the grain shipments that may have been lost. It is estimated that this strike, which has lasted since August 7, has held up the shipment of something like 38 million bushels of grain. On August 29, some 35 ships were waiting to be loaded at Vancouver. All of a sudden the Prime Minister realized the time had arrived when he must call an election. Therefore he had to act, not to save the western farmer but in an attempt to save his own political skin.
At this stage in the evolution of collective bargaining, governments should have the right to intervene with respect to commodities that are of national importance. No such provision was made in the amendments to the Canada Labour Code. The Prime Minister has not said, as the President of the United States stated when urging passage of a labour bill before Congress:
For those who argue that the government should not interfere with collective bargaining, the short answer is that the bargaining in this case has thus far failed-and failed badly for 15 months.
As I mention, Mr. Speaker, the terminal grain handlers have been engaged in collective bargaining since November 30 last. President Nixon went on to say:
I share the belief that government ordinarily should not tamper with the freedom of bargaining, but when the processes have broken down and the nation's health and safety are at stake we in public office have no right to turn our heads.
He was talking about the longshoremen's strike on the west coast of the United States. He added:
Let us resolve that this stoppage on the west coast will be the last of its kind. The Congress should act immediately to end the west coast strike and, with utmost dispatch, pass the Crippling Strikes Prevention Act.
We have nothing like that in this piece of legislation. This piece of legislation will cease to have effect on January 1, 1973. We must ask ourselves whether a strike which has not yet reached a satisfactory conclusion can be settled by January 1, 1973. I do not think it will be settled by then. The striking workers and the Maritime Shipping Association will look with anticipation to the forthcoming election to see who will be the winner. Let us say that the election is called for October 30. The declaration of the winner may take up to two weeks after that. The removal from office of those now in cabinet posts may take another two weeks. This brings us to the first part of December before a new government can take over, and then we are well into the festive season of Christmas and the New Year.

Of course, this whole subject can be dealt with when we go into committee of the whole, but I should like the Minister of Labour, the Prime Minister, and the whole cabinet to give some thought to adjusting the date of December 31, 1972 to perhaps January 31, 1973 or February 28, 1973. There is agreement by all parties in this House that collective bargaining has broken down, and everybody is anxious to pass this legislation. Today, during the question period, the Minister of Labour admitted that he knew that the Maritime Shipping Association was prepared to make a new offer to the longshoremen, but he still declared that negotiation had broken down. He must have had some inside knowledge in order to reach that conclusion, and to consider that the government needed to intervene.
We have evidence that collective bargaining with the terminal workers at the Vancouver port has been going on since September 30, 1971, so we could conclude that collective bargaining has broken down there. When we see evidence of how long it takes for collective bargaining to work, how can we, as faithful legislators, pass this legislation and expect it to work for the good of Canadians? I could not let it pass without warning this House and the country that January 1, 1973 is not an effective deadline if we think about the farmers of western Canada and the movement of grain.
But we may have an election between now and January 1, and then the Prime Minister and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) can ride their white chargers across the Prairies claiming to have solved the problem. But will the problem be solved beyond January 1? I think that the Prime Minister and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board are only thinking of themselves when asking this House to pass this legislation. The election may be November 7 or October 30 or whatever date the Prime Minister chooses, but I think they should wait until a reasonable length of time past the festive season of Christmas and New Year before allowing the legislation to lapse. Then, I would believe they were thinking of the farmers, of the alfalfa plants, the man in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon who depends on the Pacific ports to provide him with his necessary goods and commodities. I would believe that they were thinking of someone besides themselves.
A government of which I was a backbencher some years ago passed similar legislation in order to end the railway strike, but it allowed nearly six months for negotiations. The piece of legislation before us goes by the board in a relatively short period of time. I see the House Leader on the government side nodding his head in an affirmative manner.
I want the country to realize, Mr. Speaker, that the government is not making a concerted effort to keep up with the times in regard to collective bargaining. This is a temporary piece of legislation offered because they are going into an election, not because they want to save the country or help the grain farmers and people on the west coast who depend on the inward and outward flow of goods. If they are concerned with these people, then they should adjust that date to January 31, 1973. Give them 30 days after the festive season, 30 days after the election;
[Mr. Horner.)
give them to the end of March, but let us make a concerted effort to solve this difficult problem.
Reviewing the list of difficulties incurred in the labour field over the past year, it adds up to something like 400,000 man days lost in 1972 already. Having called Parliament back, are we prepared to reach some kind of conclusion which will have an effect on strikes and the economy during the difficult winter months? By January 1, 1973 we could have high unemployment, and I think the government would be wise to allow the parties involved to negotiate until the end of March, 1973 or at least until the end of February. I urge the government to consider this suggestion when we reach committee stage. Before the coming election, they must prove to the people that they have thought of the grain farmers, the lumber industry and the people who use the west coast ports. We have been called here to pass this piece of legislation, so let us do a man's job which will benefit the whole country and not just the political fortunes of the Prime Minister and the minister in charge of the Wheat Board.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the situation we face in this House and the situation at the west coast which caused us to be called together. I regard it as a very serious matter when legislators, whatever their position of power, find it necessary to impose their will on the workers and the employers in any particular sector of the nation or of industry. When we do that, we are saying to those who work that they will work for the wages they are receiving, whether they find that satisfactory or not. We are saying to employers who have machines and contracts that they shall put those machines and contracts at the disposal of the people of Canada. We would only do this I suppose, and certainly I would only consider it, if we found that there were no acceptable alternative. We are told by the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) that in effect there is no alternative.
On August 11, I wired the minister urging that mediation be used in the dispute. Somewhere around August 20 or 21, I received a reply that mediation was being carried out. As to what happened in the interim, I only know what I read in the newspapers. Following that, I assume that the minister and his officials did what they could in the way of mediating the dispute.
This House must recognize that at the base of this dispute, and surely the dispute in the St. Lawrence ports, is technological change. Until we deal with technological change, and the manner in which it affects workers and employers, we can expect to find ourselves back in this House on a similar kind of business. It is the failure to adequately deal with this technological change that causes the farmers, businessmen, working people, the citizens of Saskatchewan and, indeed, the whole prairie region, so much unease and to regard any stoppage of the movement of our products to the export markets with great concern. Saskatchewan is probably more affected than other provinces. For a number of years we have been in a sort of limbo with regard to transportation. The MacPherson commission was appointed. It finished its work and made what I regard as a largely negative report.
August 31, 1972

Since then we have been left in a situation of wondering how soon and how much of our transportation is going to be disrupted or eliminated.
A few minutes ago, the minister in charge of the wheat board made what I call his high volume wheat speech. Not too long ago, the minister arranged a deal for approximately 2,000 boxcars. I wonder how many members are aware that there are many hundreds of miles of branch lines in Saskatchewan over which these cars cannot travel. They cannot travel on these branch lines because the roadbed has deteriorated to such an extent that it will no longer support that kind of load. The railroaders and many farmers know that. I wonder how many members of this House know about it.
Thousands of farmers who normally ship their grain over these branch lines wonder how soon they will be closed and the rails pulled up. They wonder what kind of transportation facilities will then be available to them. Members of this House should not be surprised at the unease, dismay and dissatisfaction that exists among the grain growers in western Canada because of the transportation system and the lack of attention they have received from this government. That is part of the reason we are so concerned about any disruption. We do not know when the government will give more attention to these matters.
This past spring and summer we argued for better rates for rapeseed in order to be competitive. The grains group conducted a study to see what would be the next move in this game of checkers between the two main railroads and the government. A committee of the Canada Grains Council is supposed to bring in a report within the next three years. The Canada Grains Council is loaded in favour of the transportation and grain companies. The farmer will come out second best. That is why he looks with suspicion at what is being done and the way in which his interests are being looked after or, more properly, neglected. The farmer sees reports in which it is suggested there should be 80 or 90 terminals to handle the total volume of grain in western Canada. He knows that is an impractical and unworkable suggestion. When there is a tie-up at the west coast, he views this as the ultimate disaster.
There is also the matter of the movement of potash and, as another member mentioned, the products from our alfalfa pelleting plants. This affects us materially. There are hundreds of workers in these plants. I do not speak only for the farmers in my constituency. Over 60 per cent of the people in my constituency are urban dwellers. There are mine workers who work in potash plants, as well as the food and allied packing house workers who work in the meat processing plants. I am responsible to those people as well. I speak on behalf of all my constituents when I say we expect this government to conduct itself more effectively in the fields of transportation, and labour management. We expect a more effective method in dealing with disputes which arise, such as those on the west coast. We expect the government to have a better understanding of what is involved and to spend more time trying to create a better transportation system, one which will effectively serve the farmer, the business community and, indeed, the total community of western Canada.
The root of the problem is the lack of concern and understanding as to where we have arrived in this techno-
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
logical age in which we depend so completely on the smooth operation of a transportation system that must be geared to handle more products all the time, whether it is potash, grain, sulphur or coal. We must be geared to do this kind of job in labour relations, transportation, industry, and labour. The employer and the worker must assume their responsibility in this field. I am not so sure that the employer has been accepting his full responsibility. I am reluctant to tell any man how he should dispose of his time or under what conditions he should work. This is not appropriate to a free society. Nevertheless, this is what we have to do at this moment in time.

In particular, I would ask him to indicate with some clarity why the government has not yet seen fit to proclaim the Labour Code which was passed on June 30 of this year. This bill was to be the answer to the maiden's prayer as far as labour legislation was concerned. It was originally introduced by the present Minister of Manpower and Immigration. Subsequently, it was withdrawn for further study and brought in again with a number of changes. An extensive study was carried out here, yet the legislation has not been proclaimed. There may be a valid explanation.
I have some experience of this government. Ministers bring down legislation such as the tax reform bill, which is alleged to be most important. In due course it is passed. The departmental officials who devised it then come to examine it and find there are impediments to its operation. When they examine its impact on other measures, they realize that new difficulties are involved. I trust I am not being unduly suspicious, since, as I say, there may be a reasonable explanation, but among other things I would like the Minister of Labour to give the House a rational, detailed and understandable explanation of this delay in proclaiming a bill which we passed on June 30 of this year.
