speechtext:
I shall be glad to do so. I am happy to share the hon. member's expectation that any explanation I do give will be rational. The delay in proclaiming the bill which was passed here on July 5 is related principally to the question of the establishment of the new board.
As hon. members know, there is to be a new Canada Labour Relations Board comprised of at least six members. We undertook to consult extensively on this question

August 31, 1972
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
with the labour unions, management groups, persons in the judiciary who are informed on the subject of industrial relations, persons in the universities, those who are engaged in the provincial departments of labour, deputy ministers and others, and those who have been active in conciliation, mediation and arbitration procedures. I think we would all wish to be sure that this kind of broad consultation has taken place over the summer period.
I may say there has been a very generous response to our requests for suggestions concerning the new board. In the past short period the government has been considering these proposals, analyzing them and studying the question of appropriate appointments to the board. However, even when this work has been done it will take the new board some time at least in which to get itself into position. The persons who will be wanted are undoubtedly persons who are already busily engaged. Procedures will need to be established and staff recruited. A great deal of this work has already been done, though, and I hope we are not too far away from being able to proclaim the act. This is the basic cause of the time lapse.
I think it would be appropriate for me to clarify section 181 of the act which is undoubtedly in the minds of many members here. The question is whether, if the act had been in force, this section could have applied to the situation in which we now find ourselves. It is clear, in my view, that section 181 comes into play only after Parliament has been dissolved. The question becomes the following: if a dispute has reached a point at which a strike or lock-out has become legal before the dissolution of Parliament, then section 181 does not apply. On the other hand, if the dispute had not reached a point at which the seven days which must elapse after the minister has received the report of a conciliation board for a strike or lock-out to be legal, then the Governor in Council may act. It would, therefore, not apply in this situation because the seven days running time has elapsed. It was not the intention of the government, nor the intention of Parliament I am sure, as this was discussed in committee, that we put ourselves in the position of withdrawing rights which had been earned in a period before Parliament dissolved, because Parliament was there to deal with the question if it felt that the situation constituted, or was about to constitute, an emergency. Parliament was still there.
The matter was discussed and clarified in committee and I could refer to the proceedings recorded in the 25th report. The situation is, therefore, that when the seven days elapse before a dissolution use cannot be made of an order in council. When this new bill is proclaimed, in any subsequent dissolution, in any short period of two to three months occurring perhaps on an average of every four years, there is power through order in council to, as it were, postpone the lapsing of the seven days into another period. But the lapsing must begin to take place in a period between parliaments.
I shall be glad to go further into this matter if there are any questions remaining. I appreciate very much the rapid progress we have made up to this point. I feel everyone would expect me, however, to say something about the charge of inactivity which has come, in particular, from the Official Opposition. I am quite prepared to listen to this charge with respect to myself, although I

would disagree that it has application. However, I am not prepared to accept it as to the departmental officers who have long and I think recognized, experience in dispute settlement and know exactly what they are doing. I do not think it would be proper for me to let this moment go by without stating that.
Let me say first that in disputes within federal jurisdiction the experience is that over 95 per cent get settled without a strike, and many of those settlements are the result of expert work done in the department. In this particular case I want to point out that the conciliation officers were available and not fully utilized. The conciliation board was appointed and met very briefly because one party in particular did not find it useful to put a case before the board but rather wanted it out of the way, thus having stripped the situation of all the required procedures so the two parties could confront each other. They have the right to do that, and if we believe in collective bargaining we have to go along with it. You cannot force mediation. None the less, the chairman of the board remained available as did the officers of my department in Vancouver. The Assistant Deputy Minister, who is an expert in conciliation proceedings, was dispatched to the area. Subsequently, the Deputy Minister and I went to Vancouver. We have not been inactive at all and it is a mistaken notion, indeed, if one thinks he can press mediation into a situation where the parties prefer not to have it.
Let me remind the committee of the 1969 experience when another contract was being negotiated by the parties. The parties have indicated to me that at least partly because of mediation pressures three settlements were rejected by the membership. There was a strike of 39 days-with grain moving, none the less, in the ports- during which time the negotiators for the two parties came to tentative agreements. In ratification votes, those three agreements were rejected by the membership. The work resumed for three months and in the confusion that followed a fourth settlement was accepted by a very narrow margin, but only after a second strike took place. The parties, perhaps quite properly, did not want mediation pressures. That was made quite clear, and I respected that position. They felt that only by coming to grips together could they come to an agreement under which they wanted to live for the next two, three or one year period, whatever it may be. We have to keep in perspective the fact that mediation is a question of judgment and will differ dispute by dispute.
I did not want to let the occasion go by leaving any reflection on the members of the department who are so skilled and so successful as a rule in this field. I am going to consider very seriously the proposal put forward by the leader of the New Democratic Party in respect of retroactivity as it applies in the case of the grain handlers and the longshoremen's dispute. I do not know that there is anything more I might usefully say at this time. Undoubtedly, questions will arise during the committee stage and I will attempt to answer them then.

Another question which was posed and with which I thought the minister would deal related to the proposition that was put by the hon. member for Crowfoot. He said that if we are serious in wishing the parties to negotiate- and I think we all appreciate the importance and the need for collective bargaining-at the same time we should be concerned about the public interest. That is paramount. Although the parties are important, as I have indicated before many people are becoming more concerned about the fact that they are not involved in the collective bargaining process, whether they are with management or with unions. This leaves the consumer boxed in. I think that the parties must be given a fair deal in solving all their differences and I do not think that this can be accomplished by December 31.
The hon. member for Crowfoot gave several cogent reasons. He mentioned the upcoming election. He mentioned the forthcoming winter months. He mentioned the fact that it takes a new government a fair amount of time to make cabinet changes. He also mentioned the fact that before we know it we will be into the Christmas season. I can understand the confusion that may exist in the minister's mind with respect to this because we cannot be sure that meaningful negotiations will take place in the next three months or so.
After all, we know that these parties have been negotiating, I hope in good faith, for the past 10 months or so, so is it really fair to say: "If you do not reach any conclusion by way of collective agreement by December 31, you are back in the same boat again, which means you can go on strike"? They will have gone through the conciliation procedures and through the whole of the labour bill under which they are acting. We cannot afford another strike. I am asking the minister to look upon the request of the hon. member for Crowfoot with some sympathy, because I think we all want the same thing; we all want industrial peace.
I hope the minister can answer these two questions: first, whether the country will be defenceless in the event of the dissolution of parliament; and second, what is wrong with the suggestion submitted by the hon. member

for Crowfoot, who is concerned about whether there is enough time left? I hope we can be assured that the parties will bargain in good faith. Labour and management must bargain in good faith. I would like to know whether they are making full disclosure. It is obvious that either side could play hanky-panky with full disclosure.
The third point I have always concentrated upon is whether the parties are taking inflexible positions. If things have been all that tough regarding those three aspects of collective bargaining for the past ten months or so, can the minister give us some assurance that December 31 is the proper date for the ending of this legislation? How did he determine that date? I note that the employers submitted an offer prior to the introduction of this legislation. Does that offer give the minister reason to believe, after due deliberation and having listened to the advice available to him in the department, that December 31 will give ample time?
The hon. member for Crowfoot recalled, in connection with a similar bill dealing with a railway strike, that a former government provided a six months cooling off period. If a six months period was provided some years ago, have we now reached the stage in labour-management relations where three months are sufficient?
Collective bargaining is being severely tested. Many Canadians want the government to act. But the collective bargaining process cannot be easily tampered with because it provides the right to strike. That is a hard won right which nobody wants to remove. That is why I stand here with some regret. But when I analyse the situation I see that the public interest must prevail.
I have asked the minister three important questions and I hope he will give some indication of his thinking on these points.

It is a precaution and, I think, a useful one, but its suspension at this time does not expose us to the charge of being defenceless.
A question was asked about the date of December 31 and whether that is a reasonable time. This, of course, is a question of judgment. One of the considerations must be that in fact we are extending the terms and conditions of agreements that have expired, in one case for about a month and in the other case for about ten months.
I do not think we would want to extend former terms and conditions that at least one of the parties is unhappy with, since they want a new kind of agreement. We would not want to extend those any longer than we felt absolutely necessary. It would be unfair to the parties to say that they will live under those old agreements for a substantial period of time. The time should be related to the best estimate we can make for reaching a new settlement.
I would have hopes and expectations that certainly in the case of the grain handlers, where very little separates the two parties, they would quickly come to an agreement. In the other case there are complex, technological, difficult and human issues. But four months is surely an adequate time, and I would expect and hope they would make their agreement well ahead of the end of that time.
The first offers have been exchanged this week. That is a good beginning. In the government's judgment, and certainly in my judgment, the process will take several weeks. Therefore we have tried to find a reasonable balance, in fairness to all the parties involved.
I was asked whether the parties are bargaining in good faith, and I quickly answer yes. I have no difficulty in answering yes. I believe they are. The unfortunate circumstance we are all in is that by the time they got down to business, or were just on the threshhold of getting down to business, the main port on the west coast had already been shut down for 23 or 25 days. The economic situation is too clearly evident to let the strike prolong itself while the negotiations take place. So there is a cooling off period as described by the hon. member for Hamilton West which offers an opportunity to continue the bargaining.
You will note that provision is made for a mediator who will be given the authority of a conciliation board to call witnesses and to assist the parties in arriving at a settlement. It is really a question of balance. I hope we will agree that it is not an unreasonable one.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose for the dinner recess I had made a few comments about my reaction to Parliament being used in what appears to me to be a rather casual manner by the Prime Minister's summoning of the members. One day it appeared, at least to me, that he was shrugging this whole matter off as being of little consequence. The next day we received a rush summons by rather delayed telegram with little opportunity to arrive here and consider what I feel is a very serious matter for Parliament to be called back to act upon.
I suggested that the reason we are being used too frequently is that the government has been ignoring the basic issues that lie behind a developing situation such as the one with which this bill has been designed to deal. I mentioned the fact that a number of years ago Douglas Fisher, a former deputy leader of our party and then the hon. member for Port Arthur, had been involved in the events that led up to the Freedman Report.
It is true that Part V of the new labour code, which has not been proclaimed, touches lightly on some of the matters that relate to technological change. However, I suggest that the government has never considered redefining what might be described as the basic bill of rights for working people in an age when technological change is of daily concern to those involved in almost every industry, whether it lies in provincial or federal jurisdiction.
We are in danger of being called on to support a panic-button-pushing approach of the government. We had a very drastic example of that not too long ago which arose from events in the province of Quebec. I am concerned that it will become a habit of the present administration to rely on being able to draw in Parliament quickly and to

use its weight to cover its own lack of action, or the lack of action of a previous administration, in this increasingly important field.
One could go into the whole broad spectrum of a society where, with inflation and various other factors, we have an attitude taken by various segments of society which tends to hold each other up to ransom. There is an atmosphere in which one group is being pitted against another. This is as prevalent in the province of British Columbia as anywhere in Canada, though hopefully that situation may improve for the better in light of recent events in that province.
The present government should note there is a strong indication in British Columbia that people are becoming fed up with being pushed around by the kind of force that was all too prevalent in the relationship of the now retiring government of British Columbia with various segments of society, particularly with the working people who are organized into trade unions.
The cabinet in the province of British Columbia used what I call Star Chamber tactics to be able to do in secret what we are now actively doing openly. I am concerned that we may fall into that kind of trap. We should not let parliament be used for the purpose of accomplishing indirectly what poor legislation, which created a spiteful atmosphere in the province of British Columbia, has done directly by permanent authority given to the governor in council.
One aspect of this matter has been touched upon but has not been dwelt upon. Perhaps it may not be .of such broad national significance as matters such as the export of grain. I am referring to the tie-up in the coastal shipping traffic of the province of British Columbia. My observation was that they were coping with this emergency situation. When I received notice of the sitting of this House, I was in one of the northerly parts of my constituency. An airport is located there and I was able to see the airlifting and carrying of goods down the coast to fishing packers in order to ensure that essential supplies were being taken to those communities. One aspect of that matter which should not go unnoted in this chamber is that no action on the part of the longshoremen's union was taken in an effort to halt the flow of that necessary movement of commodities to the up-coast communities. I submit this reflects credit on the manner in which they have been conducting themselves in this dispute.
There is not much more I wish to say but I thought it was important I should make these remarks because I think they may help members realize that it is a group of working people in British Columbia who find themselves in this situation. They are Canadians, they have their rights, and we should not be stampeded into making sweeping generalizations or into infringing unduly upon those rights. Above all, Parliament should not be used by this government or by any other government in the future as an implement to achieve such an end.

But having listened to the reasons he gave for its not having been proclaimed, I have cause for concern and worry. When it is proclaimed the Part V now in force and effect will be repealed and the new Part V will come into force, in other words, that Part V contained in Bill C-183.

Mr. Chairman, as one who has the privilege of representing a constituency which will be affected by this legislation, both from the standpoint of those who work on the docks and that of the general public who depend for their supplies on ships, I would like to say a few words about this measure before us. I am particularly interested in the proposal made by the leader of this party this afternoon asking the government for an amendment to the bill to provide that any agreement entered into between the British Columbia Maritime Employers Association, the longshoremen's union, the grain handlers and the grain elevator companies shall be retroactive to the date when the previous agreement expired. It would be of great help to the committee if the minister could indicate whether he intends to introduce such an amendment.
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
He said this afternoon that he was sympathetic to the idea of introducing an amendment. Could we know when such an amendment could be introduced and under what clause it is going to be introduced? I think it would help a great deal if we were told that. I want to point out, Mr. Chairman, that what this committee and what Parliament face is really a contradiction in two basic principles to which most of us adhere. I think all members of the House, irrespective of party, believe in the basic principle of free collective bargaining. We believe that in a free society people have the right, either singly or collectively, to bargain regarding the terms under which they will sell their labour or their product. At the same time we also accept the principle that Parliament has a responsibility for the national welfare and to see that nt>
action taken by any single group jeopardizes the national wellbeing.
The minister this afternoon made reference to the grain sales, and the Minister of Justice again made reference to it later in the debate. I do not think enough has been said about the fact that the longshoremen's union and the grain handlers have shown a remarkable responsibility with reference to grain sales and a realization of how important grain sales are to the Canadian economy. The grain handlers have indicated their willingness to accept the conciliation report and the longshoremen's union have indicated their willingness to enter into a separate agreement to deal with grain providing the facilities were manned and operated under the National Harbours Board.
The Minister of Justice said that this was not possible, but he did not say why it was not possible. It was not possible because apparently the government was not prepared to take this rather daring and innovative step. I want to make it clear that the workers have also recognized the responsibility which they have for the wellbeing of the Canadian economy.
So Parliament is faced with these two principles: the right of free collective bargaining, and the need to protect the national well being. If, as this legislation does, we are going to remove the right to strike, then surely we have a responsibility to make absolutely sure that while protecting the national interest we do not use that as an excuse to allow the workers to be exploited or to be manipulated into accepting terms which are unfavourable to them.
Nothing that either of the ministers said this afternoon gave the immediate impression that the government is fully seized of the real cause of the dispute on the waterfront of British Columbia. The matter of wages has not been a major issue, and certainly that can be resolved. The major issue on the waterfronts of British Columbia, as it was in the eastern seaports of Canada, and as it was a few weeks ago in the seaports of Great Britain, has to do with the growing threat to the job security of the men who unload the ships. That arises out of automation, out of containerization, out of the proposed telephone computer dispatch system, all of which will change the pattern under which those who unload the ships have operated for a great many years.
It may be that changes are inevitable and that changes are desirable. We cannot be modern Luddites who try to solve problems by smashing machines or refusing to use

August 31, 1972
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
computers. But if there is to be a process of automation and cybernation then surely Parliament has a responsibility, and this government has a responsibility, first to protect the job security of workers, and second to see that a substantial share of the increased productivity arising out of automation is passed on to the general public and particularly to those who work.
This is not a new problem. The former minister of labour wrestled with this as did his predecessor. We all recall in this House the problem of the firemen on the railroads. We remember the Freedman Commission being set up and we remember the Freedman report which was accepted by all parties in the House and to which the government paid lip service, the report about which practically nothing was done. The chickens are now coming home to roost and there are going to be more problems unless we tackle this problem of technological change.
For instance, in Great Britain even the union officials wanted the men to go back to work, but they would not go back. Why? Because in three years the number of dock workers in Great Britain had been reduced by 23,000. When men get into their 50's and early 60's and see automation taking over the jobs of their fellow workers, and it keeps getting closer and closer to them, these men, who have reached an age when it is not easy to learn a new trade and to get a new job, become panicstricken. They get uptight. That is why, we have trouble in ports all around the world.
The fact that the government has this legislation here today is an admission of their bankruptcy of policy to deal with the question of technological change. What does this legislation do? It settles nothing. It does two things: one, it gets the government off the hook until after the federal election is over by sweeping the issue under the rug for four months; second, it helps the British Columbia Maritime Employers Association because after January 1 it will probably be easier to negotiate with the workers in the winter. This allows the B.C. Maritime Employers Association to get over the four big months of shipment and to negotiate after January 1, if they have not reached a settlement before then, under conditions that are much more favourable to the employers and much less favourable to the workers. The government should know that.
Therefore, it seems to me that we in this Parliament are being asked to approve legislation which is going to take away a very basic right of certain workers for the next four months. I think they are entitled to two things. They are entitled, first of all, to some assurance from the present Minister of Labour that the legislation with respect to technological change will be proclaimed, and secondly, that the government's program with respect to automation and cybernation will be stepped up, enlarged and made effective.
Additionally they have the right to know that when they do manage do work out an agreement with the employers, the Maritime Employers Association of British Columbia, that agreement will be retroactive, in the case of the longshoremen to August 1, 1972, and in the case of the grain handlers to November, 1971. That is the least to which they are entitled.

If tonight the minister can assure us that he intends to move an amendment to that effect, and tells us the clause under which he will move it, this will make it much easier for us to get on with passage of the legislation. I would like to say to him that I am sure no member in any part of the House wants to take away from any group of workers the right to strike, and we are not going to take away that right unless we provide them in return with some measure of protection, protection which in our opinion they are entitled to be given by the Parliament of Canada. Therefore I ask the minister if he can give us some information on the results of his sympathetic consideration of the proposal made by the leader of our party, and if he can assure this committee that it is his intention to move such an amendment.

speechtext:
Some of the charges range up to $4,000. This is a situation that is costing us as taxpayers something in the neighbourhood of half a million dollars a week, or about $2 million a month. This is a serious matter if only in respect to the demurrage.
Many speeches have been made in this House with respect to the movement of grain, but very little has been said about the other factors in this strike. The strike in Vancouver harbour not only ties up the movement of grain affecting the three Prairie provinces but is gradually tying up the entire economy of British Columbia.
Mines in the interior of the province, not having a place from which to move their ore, are forced to shut down. The tow boat industry which moves ore down along the shore is forced to close. Lumber operations along the coast must gradually come to a halt because there are no ships on which to load the lumber. Bit by bit, inch by inch the economy of the province is coming to a halt, involving its mines, its canneries, its forest industries, the movement of autos and other commodities coming from abroad through the port of Vancouver, as well as the outward movement of bulk commodities such as sulphur, coal and potash from the Prairies, and other bulk commodities from British Columbia itself.
In effect, basically we are looking at a national crisis involving half of Canada. I know it is difficult for members from eastern Canada to realize the importance of this to the west, and the extent of its impact upon the four western provinces, just as it is difficult for we western members to realize the importance of strikes such as the one that recently tied up Montreal harbour.
The settlement of the strike at Vancouver in the long rim will not be an easy matter. Lying at the root of the problem is the procedure with respect to dispatching gangs to man vessels. This is an old established procedure based on the hiring hall practices in the port of Vancouver. Interestingly enough the hiring hall is owned not by the union, not by a neutral organization serving both the employers and the union, but by the employers themselves. Union members going to hire on as a gang every morning come into a hall operated and owned by the employers. It is also interesting to know that this hall is the only one owned by employers and operated in this fashion on the whole of the west coast between Mexico and Alaska.
Part of the problem lies in an agreement contained in the current contract to computerize the dispatching operations. One must realize that if the dispatching were computerized, the computer now would be owned by the Maritime Employers' Association, and the union employee, for dispatch purposes, would then be at the mercy of a computer owned by his employer. If I were a longshoreman I feel quite certain that I would not want to live any longer with a practice of that kind. I think the solution would be some form of neutral hiring hall or neutral dispatching service which would serve both management and the union.
West Coast Ports Operations Bill
From my own experience and my talk with longshoremen and people working on the harbour both at management and employee level, I want to say that I believe this practice of a company-owned hiring hall is at the basis of the trouble in Vancouver Harbour. I hope that in going about the business of finding a long term settlement to the problems of Vancouver Harbour the minister will look deeply into the practices which exist in the hiring hall and the way in which dispatching is done. That is the basis of the problem we are facing today and it will not be easily solved either from the standpoint of management or the employee.
It is not an impossible question, however, Mr. Chairman. Nor is the question of computerizing the operation of dispatching on the harbour an impossible one. But the solution must be based first of all on the realization that when a longshoreman comes to be hired out to a gang in the harbour he is interested in knowing what his own position is. He wants some guarantees that he is being treated fairly relative to others hired on a gang. He wants to know that the advantages are not being weighed and cannot be weighed in the direction of management and he wants to know that the service is giving him an honest break. Because that is his livelihood.
Mr. Chairman, I say this is a human problem dealing with human relationships, with people who work very hard, honest people who are down there every day to work on that harbour and who do an excellent job in moving cargo through our west coast ports. These are not people who kick against technological improvement; in fact, they are people who recognize the advantages of technological improvement. They are not an enormous number of people; they are 1500 skilled people backed up by 1800 people of lesser skill. Their reputation is not one of striking again and again; we have had long periods of peace on the Vancouver waterfront.
At the core of the matter is the recognition that it is a human problem which must be looked at in human terms. I hope that will be the basis of any investigation to secure a permanent solution. In the meantime, it is my personal feeling that these people are prepared to stand by the bill which we will pass here asking them to continue work while a better means is found to regulate work on Vancouver Harbour. I hope we will meet in good faith, as I am sure they will meet in good faith, the question of finding a way acceptable to both sides for the regulation of this dispute.

As my hon. friend comments, he was also making remarks to save his own neck. I am in no position to judge that comment but I lay it before the committee and let the committee judge as it may see fit.
Reflecting upon the hon. member's remarks I attempted to recall when he might have spoken for the good of the country rather than in defence of the party, but could not do so. He seems to be a trouble shooter prepared to rise on any occasion. When the party seems a bit weak and needs certain defence it calls upon his superior wisdom and his comments may or may not help.
I am not trying to judge whether the party in British Columbia needs some bolstering today, nor would I like to be counted as one who suggests that this piece of legislation needs some particular defence. Having followed the hon. member's remarks closely I feel that deep down he agrees with this legislation and wants to give every opportunity possible for the normal and natural forces to work for the general advantage of the system of collective bargaining, of management and unions settling their own disputes, with the least possible government interference.
In light of that I am sure that he would be the first to agree with the amendment which I am prepared to offer to clause 5, on page 4 of the bill. I gave the purport of my amendment this afternoon. I believe that the system of collective bargaining should be given the ultimate opportunity to solve its own problems.
I believe that this piece of legislation was drawn up in haste. I could go on at length to indicate how I reached that conclusion. For example, less than 10 days ago the Prime Minister said that these people should reach then-own conclusion and asked why the government should interfere. All of a sudden, the legislation is before us.
The date suggested in this legislation, December 31,
1972.	I suggest that was not fully thought out for the good of Parliament and the collective bargaining system. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer:
That clause 5(1) of the Bill be amended by deleting the words "December 31, 1972," in line 7 on page 4 and substituting therefore the words "February 28, 1973".
I am prepared to move that amendment because I firmly believe that, in legislating a solution to any conflicting problem between labour and management, ample time should be given to the two parties to reach a satisfactory conclusion before more restrictive and demanding legislation is brought forward. If, after ample time has been given to both parties to reach a conclusion, there is no way the situation can be solved, it may be said that they need punishment, the strong arm of the law and a very firm hand to resolve the problem.
I do not want to take the time of the committee to enlarge on the point I made this afternoon, so I will briefly summarize the conclusion I have reached. We are now approaching September 1. The solution called for here will bring about the dissolution of this Parliament either tonight or tomorrow. It may well bring about the calling of an election on October 30 or November 6. It is my belief

that during the election period we will create an atmosphere in this country in which no meaningful discussion can take place with regard to this problem for which this Parliament has already formulated a solution. The two parties will want to wait until after the election to see who wins. If this government is returned to office, they may or may not negotiate. They may force further government action. If another party wins the election, they may wait to see if that party is prepared to demonstrate a spirit which will create an environment in which collective bargaining can reach a successful conclusion. I like to think that will be the case, but I may be biased.
No meaningful solution to collective bargaining will come about during a federal election. We will pass this legislation and the workers will return to work, but they will not attempt to reach any conclusion until October 30 or November 6. What will happen if there is a change in government, or a minority government with the present government still in power? There will be a period of uncertainty. A period of approximately two weeks after an election is required for the issuance of a writ to determine what party and what cabinet ministers are actually governing Canada. Another two weeks is required to appoint a cabinet. This will take us right into the festive season of December and January, January 1 in particular.
The government has been so involved in the political problem of meeting the electorate that it has failed to proceed logically step by step on this whole question. The date they have fixed is not logical. I would like to see all members of all political parties of this House unanimously agree that December 31, 1972 does not allow ample opportunity for the system to work. It does not give ample opportunity for this piece of legislation to work. It may well challenge the union to force more federal legislation upon them.
I did not reach this conclusion because of the recent turn of events in British Columbia. However, because of that, my conclusion is fortified. I ask all members to give serious consideration to this amendment. It does not change the legislation. If the strike is settled by January 1, there is no problem. The legislation will die automatically and there will be no great upheaval. If the strike is settled, the grain will be moving and commodities will be coming into and out of Canada freely, so there will be no problem. There will be no loss of face. In light of the forthcoming election and festive season, which it could be said are as sure as Christmas, why not give the system ample time to work?
Let us put partisan politics aside in this hour of urgency. Let us agree that February 28, 1973 is a far better date to include in this legislation than December 31, 1972. Let us accept this minor change in this legislation. Let us unanimously approve this bill tonight so that we can give it third reading tomorrow, face the electorate, prepare to do battle and let the electorate choose who shall govern Canada after the normal 59 days' notice is duly given. That is all I ask this House. I am not condemning the legislation. I am not condemning clause 5 or any of the prior clauses. Let us put partisan politics aside and accept this logical suggestion.

I regret I did not approach my many friends on the Liberal side and offer this amendment to them, because I know the government might then have been more receptive to the idea. Surely in this hour of crisis the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister, who saw fit to fly out government planes east and west to bring us all back to Ottawa, would agree to put partisan politics aside and accept the logic of my proposal. If they do not like the date February 28, let them agree to January 31, or March 1. Let them choose any other date. But surely they should rise and say: "January 31 is time enough; if solutions are not reached by January 31, if we are returned to this House we shall take further strong arm action".

Mr. Chairman, before we proceed with Clause 8 I think we should consider something that pertains to the future. Many of us have expressed an opinion on more than one occasion about the importance of recognizing grain as being extremely important to our national economy. Before we pass Clause 8 we should give some direction to the government in respect of the future move-
August 31, 1972

ment of grain. We realize that when there is a tie-up involving the export of grain and other commodities people begin to talk about a national disaster leading to a confrontation. I suggest that the government should accept its responsibility in this regard instead of passing it on to someone else. If the government did this there would be no reason for passing legislation to handle this type of situation.
In recognizing the extreme importance of our export markets we should consider the position of the middleman in the movement of grain. We should decide whether this man is interested in making profits from moving grain and other commodities out of the country. We might also consider the idea of nationalizing our ports and adopting a comprehensive transportation policy.
All this could be looked into by a committee vested with authority to look into the general picture and problems affecting the whole movement of cargoes through ports in Canada. It has been noted in the past that people in the port of Vancouver would rather unload U.S. goods than Canadian goods. It has been suggested that grain could be handled separately. I am sure all members of the House would agree to a study to determine the effectiveness of moving grain as an item separate from general cargo.
With those remarks I should like to move:
That Clause 8, Part II be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"provided however that before December 31, 1972, the government shall initiate a study under the Inquiries Act into the possibility of separating grain from general cargo, such grain to be handled by the Canadian Wheat Board."
There may be some question whether grain should be handled by the Canadian Wheat Board or the National Harbours Board. We support the contention that the Canadian Wheat Board should be made responsible for such handling. If it is to be responsible for moving our grain into export position and making sales, it should be given the authority to move grain through the Port of Vancouver and other Canadian ports. We recognize the importance of this situation, and this amendment would require that some consideration be given to the setting up of a study to determine a better method of moving grain out of the country.

I am not in a position to debate the question as to whether it is in order or out of order, but I preface my remarks by saying that personally I believe it is out of order. The amendment says that the government shall initiate a study under the Inquiries Act into the possibility of separating grain from general cargo, such grain to be handled by the Canadian Wheat Board. My remarks regarding the amendment were to the point. It seems to me that this is the wrong place at which to move such an amendment. The amendment should be debated at the longshoremen's union level at a particular point.
I am under the impression that there are 3,200 longshoremen at the west coast ports and something like 65 or 70 are involved in the handling and movement of grain. I am diametrically opposed to a complex situation which would involve the important matter of grain movement, which encompasses one fortieth of the total number of workers. It seems to me that this is quite wrong. I have been one who has long argued and fought against the amalgamation of various workers involved in union strikes. I believe that steel workers should be steel workers and grain handlers should be grain handlers, and that each should have the right to unionize.
